newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French LVMH strikes back at Guinness-GrandMet.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French LVMH strikes back at Guinness-GrandMet.

text.p: French luxury goods group LVMH, unhappy over the planned merger of Guinness and Grand Metropolitan, struck back on Wednesday by announcing plans to push Guinness out of their lucrative commercial ventures.

LVMH said in a statement that it was entitled by a prior agreement with Guinness to buy its stakes in their joint distribution ventures as well as Guinness' 34 percent holding in LVMH's drinks operation Moet Hennessy as a result of the merger.
Guinness said the merger did not entitle LVMH to exercise those options, signalling that the onetime allies may be headed for a court battle.
Analysts said the dispute could delay the Guinness-GrandMet merger, which would create a food and drinks giant, GMG Brands, with a market capitalisation of more than 24 billion pounds ($39 billion).

"I think it will delay and disrupt the deal with lengthy legal proceedings in prospect, and the chances of it going ahead in its current form are now much reduced," said Charles Winston at HSBC James Capel.
Analysts said LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault's move appeared aimed at forcing Guinness and Grand Met to negotiate with him.
LVMH, whose drinks portfolio includes Moet & Chandon, Veuve Cliquot and Pommery champagnes and Hennessy cognacs, owns 14 percent of Guinness.
Arnault opposes the plan to merge Guinness and Grand Met, saying only the drinks businesses are complementary.
He wanted Guinness to split its brewing and drinks activities and merge the drinks business, which includes Johnny Walker whiskies, with Moet Hennessy to form a global leader.
"A similar proposal was made to Guinness and Grand Metropolitan, and this proposal remains open for discussion," LVMH said in its statement.
"What they (LVMH) want to do is merge the wines and spirits businesses and exit Pillsbury, Burger King and the beer business," said Cecile d'Estais at Paribas Capital Markets.
With 66 percent of Moet Hennessy and 14 percent of Guinness, LVMH would be the largest shareholder of that business.
But another analyst said he did not believe Arnault would get his way. "The boards of Guinness and Grand Met don't want any more of Arnault's demands. They've purposely marginalised him," he said.
Analysts were unclear how much trouble Arnault could stir for Guinness, which helped him take over LVMH in 1990.

But the companies have drifted apart, with LVMH focussing more on luxury goods and fretting about the return on its investment in Guinness. It recently sold seven percent to help pay for the acquisition of the upscale Duty Free Shoppers chain.
LVMH said it told Guinness on Wednesday that it would buy Guinness's interest in Moet Hennessy and in the joint ventures.

"As a result, LVMH will operate the joint ventures independently, with a right to continue to market and distribute on an exclusive basis Guinness brands...in the key markets of China, France, Hong Kong, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States for at least 10 years," it said.
Analysts said the move would undercut the benefits envisaged in the GrandMet-Guinness tie-up.
"Guinness wanted to develop synergies in this area with GrandMet, with GrandMet products distributed through its ventures and vice versa. That would now seem blocked," said one analyst.
Guinness disputed LVMH's claim that the merger constituted a "control event" that entitled it to exercise the options.

"Guinness is confident that a 'control event' will not be triggered by the completion of the proposed merger, and that there is therefore no basis for the assertion made by LVMH," it said in a statement.
A spokesman said the group was confident that LVMH's action would not delay the merger, which is expected to take place in three to eight months after regulatory approvals.
Guinness' stock was down 15 pence at 580 in late trading, while Grand Met shares slipped 15-1/2 at 582.
Shares in LVMH fell 1.63 percent, swept lower by a selloff on the bourse due to nervousness ahead of the parliamentary election runoff on Sunday. The blue-chip CAC index lost 3.63 percent.
($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
